title: (ICD) Irritant Contact Dermitis
content:
Quick six template



Irritant Contact Dermatitis



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) is a reaction that takes place when the skin barrier is damaged after it is exposed to a chemical or harmful substance. The most common occurrence of ICD is on the scalp and hands of people who frequently use detergents and water, often through their work (hairdressers).



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) The symptoms of ICD are typically soreness, redness and inflammation of the affected area. The skin may also be cracked, dry and even weeping with fluid in some areas.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Lengthy exposure to detergents or water can remove the natural oils of the outer layers of the skin and cause irritation. In addition, if a damaging agent, such as a chemical, penetrates the protective outer layers of the skin, it comes into contact with the inner cells and tissues. The body reacts by attempting to neutralise the invading agent and repair the damage, resulting in the symptoms of ICD.





Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) ICD is a temporary skin reaction. It usually calms when exposure to the damaging substance is avoided, emollient cream, which makes the skin softer and/or moisturising cream.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) An emollient cream from the pharmacy or if extremely inflamed a topical corticosteroid from the GP

title: Allergic contact dermatitis Quick 6
content:
Quick six template



Allergic contact dermatitis



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Redness  – Heat – Swelling and Pain.  The reaction occurs 12-72 hours after exposure.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Sun sensitivity



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Patches of skin that are Itchy, red and blistered – type 4 reaction.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Repeated exposure to small doses of an allergen. Results from an overreaction of the body’s autoimmune system.  Many different allergens can cause this condition.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Once the body is sensitised it is for life. 



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) Avoid contact with the substance, refer to GP/Pharmacy for hydrocortisone cream, antihistamine or topical steroids.

title: Alopecia Areata
content:
Quick six template

Alopecia Areata





Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Common cause of patchy hair loss characterised by a well-demarcated shiny patch of non-scarring hair loss. 



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Short, exclamation hairs at the periphery of the lesion.



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Asymptomatic.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Autoimmune disease that is directed at the hair follicles.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) 

Unpredictable, normally resolves over time. Nail involvement (pitting). Family history of autoimmune disease. Can occur at any age. 



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) GP can prescribe steroids that are either injected or applied directly (creams or liquids) to the areas where the hair has been shed. Steroids suppress the immune cells that are attacking hair follicles, so hair can regrow.

title: Common skin conditions
content:
Common skin conditions
Conditions caused by pathogenic, hormonal & autoimmune origin
Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD)
Signs: Redness, heat, swelling, pain.
Symptoms: Itchy, red, blistered (type 4 reaction)
Aetiology: Repeated exposure to small doses of an allergen, overreaction of the body’s autoimmune system.
Prognosis: Once the body is sensitised its for life, avoid contact with substance. *
Psoriasis
Signs: Pink/silvery scaled plaques often affecting the posterior hairline and above ears.
Symptoms: Tightness of scalp, itchiness, underlying inflammation.
Aetiology: Genetic, autoimmune, stress-related.
Prognosis: May be treated but not cured. *
Tinea capitis
Signs: Ringworm of the scalp can present in various ways: Dry scaling - like dandruff but usually with moth-eaten hair loss – highly contagious.
Symptoms: Itchiness, erythema (redness) and soreness.
Aetiology: Tinea is a group of diseases caused by fungus.
Prognosis: GP referral **.  Positive prognosis once the infection is treated.
Folliculitis
Signs: Inflammation of the hair follicle.
Symptoms: Itchiness, burning and redness within the follicle.
Aetiology: Bacterial infection Folliculitis Decalvans.
Prognosis: GP referral **
Neurodermatitis
Signs: A habit of scratching, results in thickened red plaques on the anterior or posterior hair margin.
Symptoms: Intense itching.
Aetiology: Initial irritation exacerbated by rubbing or scratching, an unnoticed habit.
Prognosis: Break the habit then healing can occur.
MPHL (Male patterned hair loss)
Signs: Common hair loss, androgenic alopecia (hormonal) that beings in men after puberty.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic.
Aetiology: MPHL develops in the presence of the effect of dihydrotestosterone (DHT). This leads to MPHL whose progression is charted using the Hamilton-Norwood scale.
Prognosis: Progressive condition.  Effective treatment includes Minoxidil & Finasteride along with various Hair replacement /transplantation Finasteride tablets (type II 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor),Dutasteride.
Seborrheic Dermatitis (seb-or-riac)
Signs: Red, yellow, flaky scales.  Associated signs of nasal folds and eyebrows.
Symptoms: Inflammation and soreness.
Aetiology: Genetic/yeast infection/ stress/ temperature change (worse in winter)
Prognosis: Can be managed but is a long-term, recurring condition.
Alopecia areata
Signs: Common cause of patchy hair loss characterised by a well-demarcated shiny patch of non-scarring hair loss. Associated signs include short, exclamation hairs at the periphery of the lesion.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic.
Aetiology: Autoimmune disease directed at the hair follicles.
Prognosis: Unpredictable, normally resolves over time.  Nail pitting, family history,  autoimmune disease, can happen at any age.
Fphl Female pattern hair loss
Signs: Same as MPHL involves miniaturization of the hair follicle.  Often presents at the inner frontal hairline.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic.
Aetiology: Genetically driven.  Progression is charted using the Ludwig scale of loss.
Prognosis: No cure.  Treatment available includes minoxidil solution.  It is important to manage expectations.
Telogen effluvium
Signs: Sudden loss of hair, excess hair shedding.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic.
Aetiology: Postpartum/ Febrile illness (high temp)/ Blood loss/ Drugs/meds/ Endocrine disorders (hormonal)/ Metabolic/nutritional.
Prognosis: Normally good once treatment of the cause is implemented.  Treatment is the treatment of the cause.
Conditions caused by physical damage
trichotillosis
Signs: Self-inflected from repeated pulling/twisting/rubbing.  The most common is hair pulled from the scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes.
Aetiology: Stress-related and compulsive behaviour.  Anxiety/depression co-occurs with another habitual behaviour like thumb sucking/skin picking.
Symptoms: Sense of pleasure or relief after hair is pulled.
Prognosis: For most people hair pulling ends within 12 months, for others, it is a lifetime disorder.
Traction alopecia
Signs: Continual pulling of the hair to areas of the front and sides of the scalp.
Aetiology: Repeated consistent pulling on the hair – Ponytail/ Cornrows/ Braids/ Dreadlocks
Symptoms: Inflammation, soreness, stinging or itchiness of the scalp.
Prognosis: Many times this is not reversible unless quickly treated.  If traction continues inflammation is more widespread creating scarring and permanent hair loss.
Conditions caused by reactive chemicals
Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD)
Signs: Takes place where skin barrier after exposure to chemical/harmful substance.  Most common on the scalp and hands when using detergents frequently.
Aetiology: Lengthy exposure to detergents/ water, removes natural oils from the outer layer of the skin.
Symptoms: Soreness, redness and inflammation, Cracked/dry sometimes weeping skin.
Prognosis: Temporary reaction, avoid damaging substances and apply emollient cream.
Chemical burns
Signs: From contact, example: bleach and hair dyes.
Aetiology: On the scalp, can result in secondary cicatricial alopecia.
Symptoms: Redness, swelling, blisters, heat & pain.
Prognosis: Can result in permanent hair loss and scarring.
Thermal burn
Signs: Contact with a heated object, tongs etc. Scalding is a burn caused after contact with steam or boiling water.
Aetiology: On the scalp can result in secondary cicatricial alopecia.
Symptoms: Redness, swelling, blistering, heat & pain.
Prognosis: Can result in permanent scarring and hair loss.

title: Female Pattern HL Quick 6
content:
Quick six template



Female pattern hair loss



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) FPHL generally presents as a loss of hair volume to the mid-frontal scalp. The parting appears to be getting wider and hair overall could be feeling thinner.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)Psychological, low self-esteem



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client)Become aware of thinning around hair parting, lack of volume and loss of volume in a ponytail and overall thinning of hair throughout the head



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) It is genetically driven and it involves activation of hair follicle androgen receptors. The miniaturisation of the hair follicle occurs resulting in hair loss. Pattern hair loss (alopecia) is caused by hormones, ageing and genetics. FPHL may also be exacerbated by causes of telogen effluvium such as low ferritin (iron) levels or thyroid dysfunction



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome)There is no cure for FPHL, however, the hair loss process is not constant and usually occurs in fits and bursts. It is not uncommon to have accelerated phases of hair loss for 3–6 months, followed by periods of stability lasting 6–18 months. Without medication, it tends to progress in severity over the next few decades of life.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) 

Treatments would include: Minoxidil, topical steroids from GP, light therapy, wig or hair transplants

title: Folliculitis
content:
Quick six template



Folliculitis 



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Inflammation of the hair follicle.   A skin condition in which hair follicles become inflamed



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)Can occur anyone on hair bearing skin



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Itchiness, burning, and redness within the follicle



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Bacterial infection Folliculitis decalvans.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome)  Very good. Folliculitis is an easily treated and curable skin condition.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) GP referral

title: Frontal fibrosing alopecia uick six
content:
Quick six template



Frontal Fibrosing Alopecia



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp)Hair loss on the front and sides of the scalp



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)Eyebrows, eyelashes and other body parts



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client)Rash along the hairline and itchy/painful scalp in some cases.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) An autoimmune reaction, genetics or hormones may cause FFA



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) When the hair follicles are destroyed and replaced by scar tissue they cannot regrow.  This means your hair will not grow back.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter)Referral to GP for topical steroids cream/ointment, steroid injections may also be an option in some cases.  Treatment aims to prevent further destruction of your hair follicle but will not be able to make hair grow back that has already been lost.

title: Hair & Scalp Specialist PP
content:
Hair & Scalp Specialist
Trichology by Lorraine Hawkins
What is Trichology?  The word Trichology is derived from the Greek word ‘Trikhos” meaning hair.  Trichology is the science of the structure, function and diseases of the human hair.  In a clinical sense, Trichology is the diagnosis and treatment of disorders and diseases of the scalp and hair.- The Institute of Trichology.
Why is it important when cutting & colouring hair?
As stylists, we need to understand the hair and how it is made so we can provide a professional and quality service to our clients. It is essential that we have a basic knowledge of the hair structure and how the hair can be damaged in order for us to rectify any problems or hair disorders. This can include recommending treatments, services or products.
H a i r  S t r u c t u r e The hair has 3 layers:The CuticleThe CortexThe Medulla 
The Cuticle
In most hair types, the cuticle has 8-10 layers of flat, overlapping, translucent cells (although fine hair can have fewer).
The main role of the cuticle is to protect the inner layer cortex, so when the cuticle is damaged, it can lead to cortex damage.
The cells that make up the cuticle lie like tiles on a roof.
The direction of the cuticle cells points away from the scalp, which you can feel when moving your fingers down the hair.
The health of the cuticle is seen in how the hair feels and how it reflects light to create shine.
The surface of the cuticle is Hydrophobic(water repellent) and is physically damaged when brushing, especially when wet.
The cortex makes up 80-90% of the hair's weight, providing strength and flexibility.The cortex contains melanin, which gives hair its colour.The cortex is made up mostly of keratin, contributing to the hair's durability.The cortex reacts to chemical treatments, affecting the hair structure by penetrating the hair and breaking the disulfide bonds.
The MedullaThe medulla is the innermost layer of the hair, found mostly in thick hair.Not always present, the medulla is often absent in fine or light hair.The medulla's role in hair health or function is not well understood, as its mostly non-essential.
Pigment – 1%  Melanin, the colour pigment of the hairProtein – 78% Manly Keratin, this provides strength and structureLipids – 6% Helps to retain moisture and protect hair from drynessWater – 15%. Helps to maintain hair's flexibility and hydration
Factors that affect hair growth
Rate of hair growth and the replacement cycle may be affected by:
Nutrition – (Pic)	
Anemia
Post partum  (after having a baby)
Febrile Illness (Illness that causes fever)
Blood loss
Post operative responses (as a side effect of an operation)
Endocrine disorders (hormones/growth/metabolism)
Certain drugs and medication
Radio/Chemotherapy
Age
Gender
Genetics
Severe emotional stress
Metabolic disorders  (chemical reaction)  (a problem with how the body processes energy, nutrients or repairs it self) such as Lupus, an autoimmune disease.
Hair Types
Scalp HealthIt is important we help our clients understand the importance of scalp health.Maintaining a healthy scalp is crucial for overall hair health.We need to educate clients on: Regular cleansingMoisture balanceAvoiding excessive heatA balanced dietStress managementScalp conditions
Scalp HealthLet's look at some common scalp conditions we come across in the salon.
DandruffWhite or grey flakes appear on the hair and scalp, can be worse in winter.Very common, affecting 1in2 adultsCaused by genetic and environmental factorsNot contagious.Medicated over the counter shampoo is recommended
EczemaPatches of skin appear dry, itchy, cracked and soreNot always known what the cause is, but it is thought to be a mix of genes and environment.Triggers include allergens, soaps, stress, temperature changes and infection.Not contagious, it’s related to the immune system, not infection.Treatment includes daily moisturising using fragrance-free emollients, antihistamines and topical corticosteroids to calm inflammation.Do not colour hair if having an active flare up.
PsoriasisThick scaly plaques (silver, white or red patches)It is an autoimmune skin condition where the immune system mistakenly speeds up skin cell production.Many people do inherit a genetic riskTriggers can include infections, stress, injuries to skin (like sunburn), certain medications and cold weather.Not contagious.Moisturising helps, but medicated treatments are usually needed.There is no ”cure”, but many treatments manage it well.Do not colour hair if having an active flare-up.
Seborrheic DermatitisChronic inflammatory skin condition.It mainly affects areas rich in oil (sebaceous glands) like the scalp, face, ears and chest.It causes redness, greasy flakes, itching, and sometimes crusting.It is linked to a yeast called Malassezia that lives on the skin; it overgrows and irritates the skin, causing inflammation.It is not caused by poor hygiene.It is not contagious.Treatment would include medicated shampoos, topical antifungal cream and gentle care.
Pityriasis AmiantaceaA scalp condition causing thick, shiny scales, often sticking together to hair shafts like wax.It is not a disease itself but it is usually triggered by conditions like seborric dermatitis, psoriasis, eczema and tinea capitis.It is not contagious, but infections can sometimes occur if fungal or bacterial infections are present underneath the scaling.Removing the scales gently is important to this treatment. DO NOT pick scales off as this can damage the follicle and cause hair loss.Successful treatment depends on treating the underlying cause.
Tinea Capitis (Ringworm)Ringworm is a fungal infection, not a worm!Caused by fungus, it causes round, red, scaly patches on the scalp or skin, sometimes with hair loss in the area.It is highly contagious.You can catch it from person to person, as well as shared items (clips, combs, brushes, hats, pillows).A GP visit will be required for oral antifungal tablet treatment.If left untreated, it can cause permanent hair loss (scarring alopecia).

title: Hair_Science_and_Tricho_Care_Fundamentals
content:
Hair Science and Tricho-Care Fundamentals

Slide 1

 THE HAIR IS MADE UP OF:Lipids Pigment6% 1%© 78% Protein:2 Keratin being the hardestCysteine being the strongest15% water (or moisture)6% Lipids1% Pigments (melanin - colour pigment inthe hair)

Slide 2

HAIRSTRUCTURETHE HAIR HAS 3 LAYERS:cortexmedullacuticle

THE MEDULLAThe Medulla is a hollow cavity that runsthrough the hair, BUT not everyone hasOne and it has no function in the hair.It is also not present in fine hair.

  

 THE CUITICLEIn most hair types the cuticle has 8-10 layers of overlapping translucent cells (although finehair has less) THE CUTICLE, The main role of the cuticle is to protect the inner layer cortex, so when the cuticle is damaged, it can lead to cortex damage. The cells that make up the cuticle are like tiles on a roof.

The direction of the cuticle cells points away from the scalp, which you can feel when moving your fingers down the hair.

There is no such thing as shiny hair; only of the cuticle is in good condition will it reflect light, creating the appearance of shiny hair.The cuticle surface is hydrophobic and can be damaged if brushed when wet.

THE CORTEXT

The cortex is the inner layer of the hair, composed of protein chains.

It provides the hair with its strength and contributes significantly to its overall structure

It determines the hair's shape and texture, resulting in variations such as straight, wavy, curly or kinky.

Chemical treatments like perming, curling, straightening and bleaching penetrate the hair, breaking the disulphide bonds.

The process weakens the cortex and increases hair porosity, leading to the formation of holes and cracks which can result in brittleness and breakage.



Slide 9

HAIR IS EITHER FINE, MEDIUM ORCOARSE

Slide 10

 Hair is dead upon leaving thefollicle, and what we see today issolely influenced by the products we apply to it.Treat hair like fabric; it deserves the care of silk.

There are different strengths ofsilk for various hair types,including fine, medium, andcoarse hair. 

KERATIN

Keratin is a protein made of amino acids linked by disulfide bonds, found in hair, nails and skin.  It accounts for 80% of hair’s weight and consists of 18 amino acids.

Key Amino Acids in Keratin

Cysteine: 17.5%

Serine: 11.7%

Glutamic Acid: 11.1%

Threonine:6.9%

Glycine: 6.5%

Arginine: 5.6%



Disulfide bonds in hair

15-18% of hair consists of disulfide bonds, formed by the amino acid cysteine within the keratin protein that primarily makes up the hair structure.

Strength & Structure: Disulphide bonds are essential for hair’s strength and shape, providing the strongest linkage within the hair fibre.

Chemical Treatments: Treatments like perms and relaxers alter hair textures by breaking and reforming disulphide bonds.











Cysteic Acid in Hair

Cysteic acid forms when cysteine, a sulfur-containing amino acid in hair, is oxidized during chemical treatments like bleaching.



Impact on hair: High levels of cysteic acid indicate significant damage, resulting in brittleness, loss of elasticity, and frizz.

Detection of damage: Hairdressers assess damage from chemical treatments by measuring cysteic acid levels.

Minimising Damage: To reduce cysteic acid formation, professionals recommend using gentle treatments, proper application techniques, and post-treatment conditioning

title: Male pattern hair loss quick 6
content:
Guide to learning the scalp and hair conditions



The Quick 6: Male Pattern Hair Loss (also known as androgenic alopecia)



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Hair loss at the temples or crown of the head, single spot of baldness or hairlines receding to form an “m” shape



Associated signs: (Lesions or signs elsewhere on the body) Psychological – low self-esteem, depression and feelings of unattractiveness.



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by client) Men become aware of scalp hair loss or a receding hairline at any time after puberty, there are usually no symptoms on the scalp.



Aetiology: Cause: client thoughts first (unreliable), Trichologist’s thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) MPHL is caused by a combination of genetic and hormonal factors.  A hormone called DHT (Dihydrotestosterone) causes a change in the hair follicles on the scalp.  The hairs produced by the affected follicles become progressively smaller in diameter, shorter in length and lighter in colour until eventually the follicles shrink completely and stop producing hair.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) There is no cure, it tends to progress very slowly from several years to decades.  An early onset may lead to quicker progression.  MPHL is inherited from either or both parents.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) Treatment can include topical and oral treatments Minoxidil (slows down the hair loss if taken continuously) and Finasteride (reduces the levels of DHT), also available is wigs/hair pieces, Micro-pigmentation and hair transplants.

title: PR info Scalp
content:
Scalp health…….



Did you know that the skin on your scalp ages 12 times faster than the skin on the rest of your body and 6 times faster than the skin on your face? That is why scalp health is so important—if you want great hair you need a healthy scalp.







 



Do you have an oily scalp?...... 



Sebum, which is produced by microscopic glands in your scalp, keeps your hair and scalp moisturised; however, too much oil production can make your hair feel greasy and heavy, blocking pores.  Excessive oil production reduces your follicles' ability to produce new hair, which disrupts the hair growth cycle, resulting in hair loss.











Recommendation for good scalp health…….



Use a sulphate-free shampoo

Eat a healthy, nutritious well-balanced diet

Use a weekly hair & scalp mask

When shampooing your hair, use a massaging scalp brush.

Book a nourishing scalp treatment

title: Sebhorric Dermatits
content:
Quick six template



Seborrheic Dermatitis





Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Red, yellowy, flaky scales. 



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Nasal folds, eyebrows, armpits and groin



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Inflammation and soreness



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Genetic, yeast infection, stress-related, temperature change (can be worse in winter)



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Can be managed, but is a long-term, recurring condition.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) From the pharmacy use medicated anti-dandruff shampoo. Sometimes you may need to use a descaling preparation, like coconut oil or salicylic acid, first. Topical steroid cream may be needed from the GP.

title: Telogen effluvium
content:
Quick six template



Telogen Effluvium



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) A sudden loss of hair due to various internal factors. Excesses hair shedding.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) In rare cases hair loss on the pubic region or eyebrows



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Asymptomatic.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Telogen effluvium is a clinical sign that signals the existence of an underlying condition.  

The main causes of telogen effluvium are:



Post‐partum hair loss

Febrile illness

Blood loss

Post-­‐operative responses

Endocrine disorders

Drugs and medication

 Metabolic and nutritional disorders

Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Once treatment of the cause is implemented, the prognosis is normally good and hair growth resumes. 



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) The treatment is the treatment of the cause

title: Traction alopecia Quick 6
content:
Quick six template

Traction alopecia





Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Areas of hair loss, often to the front and sides of the scalp, that are punctuated with broken hairs. 



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Inflammation, soreness, stinging or itchiness of the scalp



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Result of repeated or constant pulling on the hair. The pulling force is usually the result of a hairstyling technique, such as a tight ponytail, which exerts an extreme pulling force on the hair and scalp.

Afro-Caribbean styling techniques tend to cause this condition. Examples include:    

Braids 

Cornrows

Dreadlocks

Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Traction alopecia in many cases is not reversible, although if the treated quickly follicles can recover, or once traction is removed from the hair, then the hair will grow back normally. However, if traction is continued, inflammation becomes more widespread and affects stem cells, which creates scarring, and permanent hair loss.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) The tight hairstyles need to be stopped immediately.  If area is inflamed an anti-biotic can be obtained from GP

When we take a holistic view of the hair andscalp, we become true professionals.By understanding the structure, the causes ofdamage, and how to care for the scalp beneath,We elevate our service from styling to science-led artistry. .

THE CONSULTATION IS WHEREPROFESSIONALISM BEGINS.It's the foundation for understanding your client’sneeds, identifying scalp or hair concerns, andbuilding trust.A strong consultation allows you to diagnoseaccurately, personalise your service, and deliverresults that truly support your client's hair andscalp health.Consultation = Connection + Confidence +Care.

ASKING THE RIGHWHAT, WHY, HOWA confident consultation begins with curiosity.Asking the right what, why, and how questionshelps uncover the underlying causes of hair andscalp issues, not just the visible symptoms.Every question should lead to understanding theclient’s hair history, habits, and lifestyle.

Slide 6

TRICHOLOGIST Vs _HAIR PRO TRAINED IN TRICHO-CAREA Trichologist is a qualified specialist who has undergone advanced clinical training todiagnose and treat hair and scalp disorders within a medical or para-medical context.A Hair Professional trained in Tricho-Care is an expert stylist or colourist who integratestrichological awareness into everyday salon practice, using their understanding of hair andscalp science to offer safe, ethical, and informed care while recognising when clinicalExpertise is required.

title: Trichocare Day 1-8 course PH1
content:
PH1 Trichocare
Day 1-8

Day 1 – Part 1: What Is Trichology?
• Trichology = the science of hair and scalp
health
• Why understanding the scalp is just as
important as styling
• What kinds of problems trichologists help
with
• Who does what? Trichologist vs
dermatologist vs stylist
• Why clients often talk to their hairdresser
first

• Day 1 part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• What do you think a trichologist does?
• Has a client ever asked you about hair loss or flakes?
• Where would you draw the line between your role and a medical professional?

Day 1 – Part 2: Hair & Scalp Anatomy
• The scalp has 3 layers: epidermis, dermis,
and hypodermis
• Hair is made of 3 parts: cuticle (outer),
cortex (middle), medulla (core)
• Sebaceous glands release sebum to keep
the scalp and hair moisturised
• Hair is mostly protein (keratin) with water,
lipids, and pigment
• Understanding this helps with choosing
treatments and recognising damage

• Day 1 part 2
• Discussion Prompts:
• Can you feel the difference between healthy and damaged hair?
• Why do you think the scalp's layers matter for product absorption?
• What happens when sebum production is too low or too high?

Day 1 – Part 3: Scalp Microbiome &
Growth Cycle
• Hair grows in 4 phases: Anagen (growth),
Catagen (transition), Telogen (rest), Exogen
(shedding)
• The Anagen (growth) phase can last 2–7 years
• The scalp has its own microbiome — bacteria
and yeast that protect the skin barrier
• Product buildup, poor hygiene, or stress can
disrupt the balance
• A healthy scalp = better hair retention and
reduced shedding

• Day 1 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• Why do you think some people shed more hair than others?
• What kinds of habits might damage the scalp microbiome?
• Can you spot when a client's hair cycle is out of balance?

Day 2 – Part 1: Hair Growth Phases &
Follicle Function
• Hair grows in a cycle: Anagen (growth),
Catagen (transition), Telogen (rest), Exogen
(shedding)
• Anagen phase lasts 2–7 years — this is
where most hair growth happens
• The hair bulb, matrix, and dermal papilla
are vital for producing new hair
• Shedding is normal — around 50–100 hairs
a day
• Illness, hormones, or stress can affect the
cycle or delay regrowth

• Day 2 Part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• What do you think causes hair to stop growing?
• Have you seen signs of excessive shedding in clients?
• Why is the follicle so important for healthy regrowth?

Day 2 – Part 2: Hair Texture, Density &
Growth Patterns
• Hair texture varies by curl pattern: Type 1
(straight) to Type 4 (coily)
• Afro, Asian, and Caucasian hair differ in
shape, thickness, and moisture retention
• Hair density = how many strands per square
inch of scalp
• Growth direction patterns include whorls,
cowlicks, and natural partings
• Elasticity and diameter affect how hair
responds to styling and breakage

• Day 2 Part 2
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you worked with all four hair types?
• Why does dense hair need different cutting techniques?
• Can you think of clients whose hair grows in a spiral or cowlick?

Day 2 – Part 3: Hair Damage –
Chemical, Physical & Environmental
• Chemical damage: caused by bleach, relaxers, and
dyes
• Physical damage: heat tools, rough brushing, and
tight styles
• Environmental damage: sun, chlorine, and pollution
exposure
• Porosity = how easily hair absorbs and retains
moisture
• Elasticity = how much hair can stretch before
breaking

• Day 2 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• What’s the most common type of damage you see in clients?
• How do you test for porosity or elasticity?
• How would you explain different types of damage to a client?

Day 3 – Part 1:
Dandruff, Dermatitis
& Psoriasis
• Dandruff: common, non-contagious, white or
grey flaking
• Seborrheic dermatitis: more severe — red,
itchy, greasy yellow flakes
• Psoriasis: autoimmune, thick red scaly
patches, often hereditary
• Eczema: itchy, dry scalp caused by irritation or
allergens
• Pityriasis amiantacea: thick silvery scales that
stick to hair shafts

• Day 3 Part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• How do you spot the difference between dandruff and dermatitis?
• Have you ever seen psoriasis on a client’s scalp?
• When would you refer someone to a dermatologist?

Day 3 – Part 2: Infections, Alopecia Types
& Trichotillomania
• Tinea Capitis: fungal infection (ringworm),
contagious via combs or towels
• Folliculitis: inflamed follicles, can be
bacterial or friction-based
• Alopecia Areata: patchy, autoimmune hair
loss
• Traction Alopecia: caused by tight hairstyles
and repeated tension
• Trichotillomania: a psychological condition
— compulsive hair pulling

• Day 3 Part 2
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you ever seen ringworm or scalp infections?
• How would you gently discuss traction alopecia with a client?
• What signs might suggest trichotillomania in a client?

Day 3 – Part 3:
Referral Boundaries
& Ethical Practice
• Know when not to treat: infections, open
wounds, or bleeding
• Language we use - safe, legal language — e.g.,
“recommend,” not “diagnose”
• Build referral relationships with GPs,
dermatologists, and specialists
• Reassure clients calmly: posture, tone, and
confidence matter

• Day 3 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you ever had to turn a client away for a medical issue?
• How would you explain a referral without alarming the client?
• Why is tone and body language important in sensitive cases?

Day 4 – Part 1: Understanding Active
Ingredients
• Salicylic acid: exfoliates and reduces flakes
— great for dandruff
• Niacinamide: calms inflammation, supports
scalp barrier
• Caffeine: stimulates circulation and may
support growth
• Peptides & botanicals: nourish and
rejuvenate scalp
• Natural oils: olive, shea, castor — protect,
soften, and seal moisture

• Day 4 Part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you used products with any of these ingredients?
• How do you explain ‘active ingredients’ to a client?
• Which of these do you think is best for a flaky scalp?

Day 4 – Part 2: Scalp Therapies & In-Salon Protocols
• Steaming: opens follicles and improves absorption
of serums and treatments
• Exfoliation: removes build-up and boosts scalp cell
turnover
• LED therapy: reduces inflammation and supports
healthy growth
• Scalp masks, oils, and serums: tailored to client
needs
• Know your contraindications: don’t treat open
sores, infections, or broken skin

• Day 4 Part 2
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you ever used steam or LED therapy in the salon?
• What’s your go-to scalp treatment for dryness or flakes?
• When would you avoid treating a client’s scalp?

Day 4 – Part 3: Massage
for Circulation &
Relaxation
• Scalp massage increases blood flow to
the follicles
• Promotes nutrient delivery and may
support hair growth
• Helps relieve stress and tension in
clients
• Boosts the effectiveness of products
like oils and serums
• Use a gentle, confident technique —
pressure, rhythm, and consistency
matter

• Day 4 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you tried incorporating massage into your services?
• How does a client typically respond to a good scalp massage?
• What makes a massage feel professional instead of awkward?

Day 5 – Part 1: Hair Types, Shapes &
Ethnic Variation
• Asian hair: thick, straight strands with
round follicles and high density
• European hair: oval follicles; varied
diameter and wave patterns
• Afro-textured hair: tight curls, flat elliptical
follicles, fragile and dry
• Follicle shape determines curl pattern,
elasticity, and strength
• Hair type affects product absorption,
moisture retention, and breakage risk

• Day 5 Part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• Which hair type do you find most challenging to treat or style?
• How would you adapt techniques for different hair types, such as fragile and dense hair?
• Why is it essential to recognise ethnic variations in hair care?
• How do you adapt products for different hair types?
• What texture or curl pattern do you work with most?

Day 5 – Part 2: Growth
Patterns & Tension Zones
• Scalp patterns: crowns, cowlicks, and whorls affect hair
direction and styling
• Growth direction impacts tension, partings, and cut
results
• Tension zones: temporal, crown, and occipital areas
prone to traction stress
• Tight styles (e.g. braids, weaves) can cause tension
damage
• Use mapping and gentle styling to reduce breakage risks
• Protective styles must balance aesthetics with long-term
scalp health

• Day 5 Part 2
• Discussion Prompts:
• How do you adapt styling for clients with strong growth patterns?
• Where do you commonly notice tension-related thinning?
• How do you educate clients on safe styling habits?
• How can we style tighter hair types without causing damage?

Day 5 – Part 3: Analysing Texture,
Porosity & Elasticity
• Porosity test shows how hair absorbs and
retains moisture: low, normal, or high
• Elasticity test reveals strength and flexibility
— snap vs stretch = moisture vs protein
• High porosity hair absorbs quickly but dries
fast — often damaged or over-processed
• Product build-up can distort results —
clarify before testing
• Shrinkage, frizz, or snapback offer visible
cues for client education

• Day 5 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• How do you check for porosity or elasticity during a consultation?
• What signs help you decide if hair lacks protein or moisture?
• How do you explain moisture vs protein needs to clients?
• What small tests can help you understand hair condition

Day 6 – Part 1: Key Nutrients for Hair
Growth
• Hair is non-essential tissue — signs of nutrient
deficiency appear early
• Iron, Zinc, Vitamin D3, B12: vital for healthy follicle
function and cell turnover
• Protein supports keratin synthesis — low intake = excess
shedding
• Biotin only benefits hair if a deficiency is present — not
a miracle cure
• Hydration and antioxidant-rich foods help maintain the
scalp barrier and reduce inflammation
• Protein is essential — hair is made of keratin
• Crash dieting or dehydration can show up as dullness or
shedding
• We can’t diagnose, but we can raise awareness and
recommend speaking to a GP

• Day 6 Part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you noticed how diet affects your own hair?
• How can we discuss nutrition without stepping outside our role?
• What signs suggest a client may have a nutritional deficiency?
• How could you ask about nutrition without overstepping?
• What signs suggest internal stress rather than external damage

Day 6 – Part 2: Hormonal Imbalances &
Hair Shedding
• DHT (a form of testosterone) contributes to
male/female pattern hair loss
• Menopause: drop in oestrogen leads to
follicle shrinkage and thinning
• PCOS: high androgens and insulin resistance
can trigger shedding
• Postpartum hair loss = Telogen Effluvium
due to hormone fluctuations
• Thyroid disorders slow regrowth and alter
hair texture and density

• Day 6 Part 2
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you seen hormonal changes affect your own or clients’ hair?
• How would you explain Telogen Effluvium to a worried client?
• What are respectful ways to suggest someone might need medical tests?

Day 6 – Part 3: The Impact of Stress,
Sleep & Habits
• High cortisol from chronic stress can push
hair into resting (telogen) phase
• Poor sleep disrupts scalp repair, growth
signals, and barrier recovery
• Gut health and inflammation may trigger
autoimmune-related hair loss
• Smoking, alcohol, and crash diets reduce
blood flow and nutrient supply to follicles
• Stylists can help spot lifestyle-related
triggers during consultation

• Day 6 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• Have you seen links between stress and sudden hair changes in clients?
• What lifestyle habits would you gently ask about during a consultation?
• How can we stay supportive without sounding judgmental?

Day 7 – Part 1: Building Trust Through
Consultation
• Consultation goals: gather info, educate the
client, build reassurance
• Tone, posture, and empathy establish
immediate rapport and safety
• Key intake info: health history, lifestyle,
medications, allergies
• Open vs closed questions: use open ones to
explore and build trust
• Respect client privacy — know GDPR basics
around data handling

• Day 7 Part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• What questions help you build trust during a first appointment?
• How can tone and body language affect a nervous client?
• Why is health and lifestyle information important for scalp care?

Day 7 – Part 2:
Allergy Testing &
Observation Tools
• Always follow brand guidelines for allergy
testing (e.g., 48-hour patch test)
• Use Colourstart if trained and permitted —
not a replacement for GP testing
• Look for signs: redness, flaking, sores — don’t
diagnose, observe
• Use a dermatoscope or phone camera (if
appropriate) for monitoring
• Keep simple notes: what you see, what you
recommend

• Discussion Prompts:
• How do you explain the importance of allergy testing to clients?
• Why is it helpful to visually track a client’s scalp changes?
• What do you look for during a scalp check before colouring?
• When would you avoid working on someone’s scalp?
• What language helps you stay safe legally and professionally?

Day 7 – Part 3:
Reviewing Results
& Maintaining
Engagement
• Review progress using consistent photos, notes, and
consultation forms
• Set clear timelines — hair/scalp improvements often take weeks
to months
• Stay honest but supportive: manage expectations kindly
• Address sensitive issues (stress, alopecia) with empathy and
discretion
• Know when to refer again or adapt the current treatment plan

• Day 7 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• How do you handle clients who expect instant results?
• What’s your strategy when a treatment isn’t working?
• When should a client be referred again to a medical expert?
• What helps you manage client expectations over time?
• How can you stay supportive when clients are emotional?

Day 8 – Part 1:
Becoming a
‘Scalp-Aware’
Hair Professional
• Use trichology knowledge to build trust — not to diagnose
• Spot common scalp issues and explain concerns using safe language
• Document client concerns clearly without making clinical claims
• Refer to medical experts when issues fall outside your role
• Offer scalp-focused consultations to elevate client experience

• Day 8 Part 1
• Discussion Prompts:
• What language would you use to refer a client without overstepping?
• How could a scalp-care focus help you stand out as a hairdresser?
• Have you ever treated someone who really needed to see a specialist?

Day 8 – Part 2: Creating Simple Scalp
Care Services
• Offer cleanse, exfoliate, massage, and
moisturise treatments safely
• Use non-medical tools: steamer, scrubs,
calming serums, natural oils
• Create short scalp rituals as luxury add-ons
or standalone services
• Price based on time, product use, and value
— not 'treatment claims'
• Know when NOT to treat: open wounds,
active infections, unknown reactions

• Day 8 Part 2
• Discussion Prompts:
• Which treatments do you already offer that could benefit the scalp?
• What’s one simple scalp ritual you could create for your clients?
• How can you make this feel luxurious without crossing clinical boundaries?

Day 8 – Part 3: Building Confidence &
Conversations
• Use consultation forms to naturally
introduce scalp discussions
• Educate clients with simple terms: build-up,
flaking, dryness, shedding
• Take photos to show progress — builds
trust and client satisfaction
• Promote scalp services with ethical wording
and disclaimers
• Continue learning: partner with
trichologists or refer when needed

• Day 8 Part 3
• Discussion Prompts:
• What stops professionals from offering scalp care confidently?
• How can you promote these services without sounding medical?
• Would you consider collaborating with a trichologist in future?

title: Trichology Info
content:
What is Trichology?;



Trichology involves the study of hair growth, structure and function, as well as the diagnosis and treatment of hair & scalp disorders.



Trichologists are qualified to give advice on haircare practices and prescribe appropriate treatments or therapies to promote healthier hair and scalp.



Did you know that half of all clients are suffering from some form of thinning hair or hair loss? That’s a whopping 50% of people sitting in your chair who need advice and support, Trichology is therefore an important part of a stylist’s education to best support our clients.





When should your client see a Trichologist?



The client has persistent or severe hair loss

The client has unexplained changes in hair texture or quality

Allergic reactions or sensitivity

Suspected scalp or hair disorders

- Day 8 – Part 3: What You Can (and Can’t) Say or Do
- Stylists: observe, recommend, refer, educate
- Avoid diagnosis; use safe language
- Get insured for scalp care services
- Use disclaimers & patch-test waivers
- Continue CPD, clinical trichology pathways

title: Trichotillosis
content:
Quick six template



Trichotillosis



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) It is a self-inflicted condition that arises from repeated pulling, twisting or rubbing of strands of hair. The most common site of hair loss is the scalp and hair looks twisted and fragmented.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Hair loss to Eyelashes and eyebrows



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Sense of pleasure or relief after hair is pulled



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Stress-related and compulsive behaviour.   Psychological factors especially in children (stress reduction, emotional regulation, sensory stimulation)



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) For most people, the hair pulling ends within 12 months. For others, trichotillomania is a lifelong disorder.

Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) Seeking treatment for depression, anxiety, or poor self-image often will improve the hair pulling and negative feelings

title: Tricocare PH1 Exam Day 1-4
content:
Tricocare PH1 – Comprehensive Multiple Choice Exam

Answer all 20 questions. Circle the BEST answer for each. This paper covers content from Days 1 to 4.

1. Which of the following best explains why clients often ask stylists about scalp issues?

A. Stylists are medically trained to treat scalp disorders

B. Salons are more accessible than clinics

C. Hairdressers see the scalp more frequently than GPs

D. Clients trust stylists' product recommendations more than doctors'



2. What is the function of the dermal papilla within the hair follicle?

A. It produces sebum to coat the hair

B. It provides blood supply to support hair growth

C. It controls melanin production in the medulla

D. It anchors the follicle in the hypodermis



3. Which component of the hair strand contributes most to strength and elasticity?

A. Medulla

B. Pigment granules

C. Cortex

D. Cuticle



4. Which of the following would most likely disrupt the scalp microbiome?

A. Mild herbal shampoos

B. Regular brushing

C. Overuse of harsh chemical products

D. Warm water rinses



5. What is the typical duration of the anagen phase for scalp hair?

A. 2–3 weeks

B. 2–7 years

C. 1–2 months

D. 10–15 days



6. What makes Type 4 hair particularly prone to breakage?

A. Low density

B. Oval follicle shape

C. High elasticity

D. Tight curl pattern with fewer cuticle layers



7. Which statement is TRUE about follicle miniaturisation?

A. It results in stronger, thicker hairs

B. It is always caused by trauma

C. It leads to shorter, finer regrowth

D. It permanently damages the cortex





8. What does high hair porosity usually indicate?

A. Cuticles are tightly sealed

B. Hair holds moisture for long periods

C. Cuticles are lifted or damaged

D. The medulla is overactive



9. Which condition is associated with autoimmune causes and patchy hair loss?

A. Traction Alopecia

B. Alopecia Areata

C. Folliculitis

D. Tinea Capitis



10. Why should stylists avoid diagnosing scalp conditions?

A. It's unnecessary; most conditions resolve on their own

B. It could delay the client receiving proper medical care

C. Clients prefer home remedies

D. Insurance covers stylist diagnoses



11. Salicylic acid is classified as which type of compound?

A. Alpha hydroxy acid

B. Protein bond relaxer

C. Beta hydroxy acid

D. Emollient oil





12. What is the role of caffeine in scalp treatments?

A. Acts as a cleansing surfactant

B. Enhances elasticity of the cortex

C. Stimulates circulation to the follicle

D. Blocks hormone-related hair loss



13. Which ingredient is best known for barrier support and reducing inflammation?

A. Shea butter

B. Castor oil

C. Niacinamide

D. Sulphur



14. Which of the following is NOT a contraindication for scalp therapy?

A. Infected lesions

B. Scalp psoriasis flare-up

C. Recent open wound

D. Healthy dandruff-free scalp



15. What distinguishes seborrheic dermatitis from simple dandruff?

A. Seborrheic dermatitis causes less irritation

B. Dandruff flakes are red and greasy

C. Seborrheic dermatitis includes redness and greasy yellow flakes

D. Dandruff is contagious



16. Which practice can help maintain a healthy scalp microbiome?

A. Frequent bleaching

B. Avoiding all hair products

C. Using pH-balanced cleansers

D. Exfoliating daily



17. What is the safest way to approach a suspected scalp infection in a client?

A. Recommend antifungal shampoo immediately

B. Provide a deep cleansing mask

C. Refer them to a medical professional promptly

D. Continue treatment with gloves on



18. Why is massage included in scalp care treatments?

A. It removes toxins from the bloodstream

B. It stimulates nerves in the medulla

C. It promotes relaxation and circulation to the follicle

D. It closes open pores after exfoliation



19. What is the correct legal language to use when advising a client about a scalp concern?

A. 'I think you have eczema'

B. 'Let me diagnose that for you'

C. 'I recommend seeing a specialist about this'

D. 'You have psoriasis for sure'

20. Which therapy is designed to boost scalp cell turnover by removing dead skin layers?

A. LED therapy

B. Exfoliation

C. Steaming

D. Tension massage
